title: OdysSim: Building Foundation Models for Human Behavior Simulation
claim: Our small open model matches or beats much larger frontier models across many behavior-simulation benchmark categories.
layout: 6 bar-chart panels in 2x3 grid, our purple bar highlighted rightmost
description: A 2x3 grid of rounded cards, each a bar chart for one task category: Conversation, Social Skill, Cognition, Role Play, Evaluation and Agent-User. Small pill tags under each title list the datasets in that category. Each card has six bars with the score printed above each bar and a model logo at its base. Baselines are GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, Qwen 3.6 Plus and Qwen3 8B Instruct. They are drawn in a gradient from dark navy to pale lavender. The rightmost bar, Osim 8B, is saturated purple with a bold purple label. It is the tallest in Conversation (56.5) and Social Skill (49.2). It is competitive but not best in Cognition, Role Play, Evaluation and Agent-User. The eye goes first to the purple bar at the right of each panel.
caption: Benchmark results on human simulation tasks.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as human simulators for interactive evaluation and social simulation. Yet helpfulness-driven post-training pulls them toward a homogeneous, overly agreeable assistant register, creating a behavioral Sim2Real gap. We present OdysSim, the largest open systematic investigation of behavioral foundation models, i.e., models trained to simulate human behavior at scale. We propose SOUL, a taxonomy of five capability axes (CONV, SS, COG, ROLE, EVAL) that unifies 62 datasets and 23 benchmark tasks under one framework. Specifically, we curate the OdysSim corpus (21.4M interactions, 10B tokens, retrofitted with back-generated social contexts), construct the SOUL-Index benchmark, and develop an end-to-end training recipe combining midtraining, task-specific RL, and expert distillation. The resulting open 8B OSim model ranks first or tied-first on 8 of 23 tasks, outperforming any individual frontier model by this count, with the strongest gains on conversational and social tasks. Its outputs are also more human-like in length, formatting, and word choice, and it transfers zero-shot to out-of-distribution user simulation on $Ï$-bench, nearly matching real users on reaction alignment (93.2 vs. 93.5). We further show that LLM-as-judge RL induces reward-hacking patterns, and that our detectors can mitigate them during post-training. Together, our findings suggest that behavioral foundation models require rethinking the LLM training paradigm. We release all artifacts to support future research.
